implementation_notes: Ruby loads a file at most once per process: Kernel#require consults $LOADED_FEATURES and returns false instead of re-executing, so code at the top level of a required file is the built-before-use form (the Kernel documentation words it as 'loads the given Ruby file unless it has already been loaded'). Deferred construction is the memoizing `@config ||= build_config` idiom, and `autoload` defers loading a constant until it is first referenced. There is no guard object or counter; the real questions are path identity and thread safety.
code_sketch:
# config.rb
CONFIG = Config.new           # executed once, on first require

class Service
  def config
    @config ||= Config.build  # memoized first use per instance
  end
end
pitfalls: require is keyed by resolved path: the same file reached through a different real path (symlink, changed load path) is loaded twice, producing two constants and two instances.
`||=` is not atomic on all runtimes (JRuby, TruffleRuby, and plain threads): two threads can both build the value, and it recomputes whenever the stored value is nil or false.
load re-executes the file by design; using it where require is intended re-runs top-level construction, which is the classic source of duplicated state in development reloaders.
autoload resolves the constant on first reference, so an error inside the autoloaded file surfaces in unrelated code, and its thread behaviour is not something to rely on.
